title: Transferable SCF-Acceleration through Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning
claim: Models trained on standard targets degrade out of distribution, while solver-aligned training keeps consistent gains across a wide range of sizes.
layout: 1 wide line plot, shaded OOD regions, dotted baselines vs solid ours
description: A single wide line plot. The x-axis is the number of heavy atoms, from about 4 to 90. The y-axis is Effective Relative Iteration Count on a log scale from 0.6 to 4.0. Gray background bands mark the QM9, QM40 and QMugs regimes, and an arrow along the bottom labels the out-of-distribution range. A horizontal line at 1.0 separates 'Slowdown' (red text) above from 'Speedup' (green text) below. Three colors stand for three model types: orange for density, green for Hamiltonian and blue for coefficients. Dotted lines with open markers are baselines and solid lines with filled markers are SAIL. Shaded bands show variability. The dotted matrix baselines climb to 2–3× slowdown. The solid SAIL curves stay flat near 0.65–0.8. The legend sits across the top.
caption: \textbf{Size extrapolation of \ours{} on B3LYP / def2-SVP.} ERIC of initial-guess models trained on QM9 and evaluated on QM9, QM40, and QMugs, with QMugs molecules up to $10\times$ larger than those seen during training. ERIC $< 1$ indicates speedup over the traditional initial guess, ERIC $> 1$ slowdown. Matrix-models trained on ground-state targets degrade out of distribution, whereas \ours{} maintains a $\sim 25%$ speedup across the full range. The coefficient model is robust out of distribution, yet every \ours{}-trained model (matrix variants included) outperforms it across the full range.
abstract: The cost of Kohn-Sham density functional theory (KS-DFT) calculations scales with the number of required solver iterations, which depend on the quality of the initial guess. Machine learning methods that predict initial guesses from molecular geometry can reduce this cost, but matrix-prediction models fail when extrapolating to larger molecules, degrading rather than accelerating convergence [Liu et al., 2025]. We show that this failure is a supervision problem, not an extrapolation problem: models trained on ground-state targets fit those targets well out of distribution, yet produce initial guesses that slow convergence. Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning (SAIL) resolves this for both Hamiltonian and density matrix models by differentiating through parts of the self-consistent field (SCF) solver end-to-end. We introduce the Effective Relative Iteration Count (ERIC), a correction to the commonly used RIC that accounts for hidden Fock-build overhead. On QM40, which contains molecules up to 4$\times$ larger than the training distribution, SAIL reduces ERIC by 40% (PBE), 35% (SCAN), and 32% (B3LYP), more than doubling the previous state-of-the-art reduction on B3LYP. On QMugs molecules 10$\times$ larger than the training set, SAIL delivers a 1.35$\times$ wall-time speedup at the hybrid level of theory, extending ML SCF acceleration to large drug-like molecules.
